events.text: It comes to you on the wind from three provinces away, so faint that at first you take it for water over stones: stone chimes, then bronze bells, then a long line of bamboo pipes. Somebody is playing the Shao, the music of the sage-king of the old books, the music that is played in nine movements to call the phoenix. Nobody has played it properly in a thousand years. Somebody is trying.

choices.text: Fly toward it now, before it stops

effects.log: You fly three days with the music getting louder. It stops and starts again each morning: a court rehearsing. By the time you see the roofs of the capital you could hum the third movement yourself.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge and listen to all nine movements first. Is it true all the way through?

effects.log: You listen for a whole season. Eight movements are true. The ninth has one note in it that is wrong every time, the same note, in the same place, as if somebody means it.

choices.text: Sing one note back to it from the ridge, with your mate, and see who answers

effects.log: Two voices, one note, three provinces. The next morning the court musicians begin the whole piece again in your key. Somebody down there heard, and is very frightened, and very glad.

events.text: You come in over the capital unseen and fold yourself into the curve of the roof ridge above the great courtyard. Below, the court music is laid out like a field: stone chimes hung in two rows of eight, bells on lacquer frames, a tiger-shaped scraper, pipes and zithers, and sixty-four dancers in red holding a flute in one hand and a pheasant's tail-feather in the other. The king sits on the dais. Every courtier in the yard is looking at the sky and pretending not to. They are at the seventh movement.

choices.text: Wait for the ninth, as the old books say

effects.log: You wait. The seventh movement, the eighth. A minister faints in the heat and is carried out by his feet. The dancers lift their feathers all together, and you feel your own tail lift, as if it had been asked.

choices.text: Look into the orchestra instead of at the king

effects.log: Sixty-four dancers, forty musicians, and at the end of the row of flutes an old player with a white topknot whose face is wet. Nobody else has noticed. Musicians cry at music. This is not that.

choices.text: Look at the dais, at the stones under the throne

effects.log: The dais is new stone set on old stone. Where they meet, a drain-hole, and in the drain-hole a little bunch of wildflowers that somebody has pushed in from the back, where the servants walk.

events.text: The ninth movement. The stone chimes are struck from the lowest to the highest, and the whole court holds its breath, and you come down out of the sky into the courtyard and stand in the measured dance, as the books say you would. The dancers do not stop. The king rises. And in the ninth bar, at the place you knew it would be, one flute plays the wrong note, very clearly, on purpose, and its player is weeping.

choices.text: Dance it through to the end. The music is not the player's alone

effects.log: You finish the measured dance on the flagstones with the whole court on its knees. The heralds are writing before you leave the yard. The old flautist has stopped playing and is looking at you as if you had stepped on something.

choices.text: Stop in the middle of the dance and turn to the flautist

effects.log: You stop. Sixty-four dancers stop with you. You and the old player look at each other across the yard, and the court does not know where to look, and so, for once, it looks at the flautist.

choices.text: Rise back to the roof before the last bar

effects.log: You are gone before the music ends. The court argues for a month about whether it saw anything. The old flautist does not argue. The old flautist looks up at the roof every evening, at the place you sat.

events.text: That night you come down the eaves to the musicians' quarters in the shape that can speak. The old flautist, {npc}, is sitting on the step with the flute across {his} knees and is not surprised. "You heard it," {npc} says. "Good. Somebody had to." {He} touches the flute. "This hall was built over a well. The old king's grandson was drowned in it, nine years old, the night this king took the seal. I taught the boy to play. The note I play wrong is the note the boy could never get right."

choices.text: "Is there proof, or only grief?"

mem.note: asked me for proof, not pity

effects.log: "The flowers," {npc} says. "In the drain under the dais. The boy's nurse puts them there every month. Ask the nurse why. The nurse will not tell you. Watch the nurse's face when you ask."

choices.text: "I heard the note. I will not forget it"

effects.log: {npc} breathes out as if {he} has been holding the breath for nine years. "Then it was worth it," {he} says. "Whatever they do to me."

choices.text: "It is not for a bird to judge kings"

effects.log: "No," {npc} says. "Only to stay or go." {He} picks up the flute. "That is judgement enough, I think. Good night."

events.text: You watch the throne hall for a season. The flowers in the drain-hole are changed on the first of every month by an old woman with a servant's bucket who never looks at the dais and always cries on the way back to the kitchens. At night, when the hall is shut, the king comes alone and stands over the drain-hole for a long time, and goes away without praying.

choices.text: Fly down in broad daylight and stand on the stone over the drain-hole

effects.log: The whole court sees the phoenix of the ninth movement walk to the dais and stand on one particular stone and look at the king. Nobody says the word well. By evening the whole capital is saying it.

choices.text: Keep watching. The king who stands at night over the drain is not finished deciding

effects.log: You watch another year. The king has the old woman given a pension and a house outside the walls. He does not stop coming at night. You do not know yet whether this is guilt or only fear, and you are not sure there is a difference.

choices.text: Ask your mate what they see

effects.log: Your mate watches the king a whole night and says: "He would undo it, if it could be undone. It cannot. That is the crime now: that he keeps the seal." It is better than anything you had thought.

events.text: A year later the court plays the Shao again, all nine movements, to call you back. And standing among the guards in the courtyard is one human the others step round without knowing why: a master of the martial world, old, very still, strong enough to see what heaven sees. When you come down at the ninth movement, that one looks straight at you, and you understand that you could ask, and be answered.

choices.text: Ask: "We have come. Must we stay?"

ok.log: The old master answers aloud, in the middle of the court music, so that the king hears it: "Not while the well is under the throne." The music stops. Nobody arrests the old master. Nobody dares.

fail.log: The old master looks at you a long time and says nothing at all. Perhaps the answer is that it is not for humans to say. Perhaps the old master is afraid. You will have to decide this yourself.

choices.text: Do not ask. A phoenix that needs to be told has not been watching

effects.log: You stand in the dance and look at the old master, and the old master bows very slightly, as one craftsman to another, and does not speak.

choices.text: Let your mate ask, and you listen to the answer

effects.log: Your mate asks. The human answers quietly, only to the two of you: "A good king, in every way but one. The one is under the dais." Your mate looks at you. Now you both know.

events.text: The tenth movement. There is no tenth movement in the old books. The court musicians play the ninth again, because you have not gone, and then again, and the dancers' arms are shaking and the king is grey. You stand on the flagstones. You can stay. You can go. You have stood in this dance before in other courts; you have never stood in it over a grave.

choices.text: Rise from the courtyard in full sight, and fly away over the wall

effects.log: You go up over the bells and the chimes and the dais and away north. Behind you, alone, a single flute plays the boy's note right, for the first time in all those years. Within the year the king gives up the seal to the boy's cousin and goes to live in a temple. Nobody says why. Everybody knows.

choices.text: Stay. The king is good in everything but one, and the land is fed

effects.log: You stay in the dance until the music runs out. The heralds go out on every road. The granaries stay full and the roads stay safe and the flautist never plays again, and something in your breast feathers is never quite clean after. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Go down to the drain-hole and sing over it, once, for the boy

effects.log: You sing the boy's note over the drain-hole in front of the whole court. The king comes down off the dais and kneels on the stones beside you and does not get up. The next spring they dig out the well and bury the child in the royal hills with a flute in his hands.

choices.text: This is a reign you graced once. Taste the palace spring, and say what it tastes of

effects.log: You drink from the spring in the palace garden in front of the court. Iron. You lift your head and let them see you taste it. The reign you blessed has gone bad from underneath. Now you have to leave it in time, or stay and dull.

events.text: The new throne hall has its roof on and its ceiling bare. In the yard the master carvers argue over a drawing: two phoenixes facing each other among clouds, to hang above the throne, as the old halls had. The youngest carver says nobody alive has seen a phoenix, so they should copy the old hall. The oldest says the old hall's birds look like geese. They have built bamboo scaffolding to the ceiling, and they look up at it, and they look at the sky.

choices.text: Sit for them: land on the scaffolding at dawn, very still

effects.log: The oldest carver drops a chisel forty feet and does not notice. Nobody in the yard breathes. You sit on the top pole of the scaffold until noon, and when you go, every carver has drawn you, and none of the drawings is any good.

choices.text: Sit only in the hour before dawn, when the hall is empty but for the carvers

effects.log: For a month, in the grey hour before the court wakes, you sit on the ceiling beam and the carvers work by lamplight with their mouths shut. A palace guard sees you once and is told by the carvers that guard was dreaming.

choices.text: Refuse. A bird is not a carving, and a throne is not a branch

effects.log: You fly over the yard without stopping. The carvers copy the old hall. The birds look like geese. Every king who sits under them for three hundred years is faintly embarrassed and does not know why.

events.text: The master carver, {npc}, has a problem. Two birds face each other on the drawing, but whenever the carver looks up from the block there is only one phoenix on the beam. Look down, and there are two shadows on the floor. Look up: one. "Is it two birds," {npc} asks the empty hall, "or one bird very quick?" {He} is too old a craftsman to carve what {he} cannot see.

choices.text: Sit with your mate, side by side, as still as wood, for a whole morning

mem.note: saw both birds at once, once

effects.log: For one morning {npc} looks up and there are two. {He} carves without stopping to eat, and at noon there is one again, and {he} laughs out loud in the empty hall. "I have you," {he} says. "Both of you. Go on, then."

choices.text: Take turns on the beam, one dawn each

effects.log: {npc} carves one bird on the even days and the other on the odd. The two are not the same bird. When they hang facing each other, they look like an old couple in the middle of a quarrel, and it is the best thing in the hall.

choices.text: Sit alone, and let {him} invent the second bird

effects.log: {npc} carves you true and carves the second bird from your shadow and a long life of looking at things. It is not anyone you know. It is whoever {npc} has missed most. You never ask who.

events.text: The carved birds go up, gilded and painted in the five colours, and something goes up with them. You feel it the first winter: when the throne hall is cold you are cold, a little, across the back; when they light the braziers under the dais you are warm. Some of you went into the wood with the carver's chisel and did not come back out.

choices.text: Let it be. A little of you over a throne is not a bad place for it

effects.log: You learn to feel the hall the way you feel weather. Who comes in, who kneels, who lies. It is like having a second, very slow eye, set fifteen times a man's height above the floor.

choices.text: Go back and sit on the carving until you have pulled yourself out of it

effects.log: It takes a winter of sitting on your own carved back in the dark. Most of you comes out. Not all. (-10 health)

choices.text: Your mate feels it too. Keep the warmth as a thing the two of you share

effects.log: When the braziers are lit in the hall you both shift on the branch at the same moment, a hundred li away, and look at each other. Nobody else in the world knows what that means.

events.text: The first king to sit under the carved birds is crowned on a wet spring morning. You feel the hall fill. When the court has finished bowing and the young king is alone on the dais for one moment, the king looks up, straight up, for a long time, at the two birds among the clouds, the way a child looks at the stars to see whether they are looking back.

choices.text: Let the carving be warm under the king's gaze

effects.log: The young king feels it, the way you feel sun through a paper door, and smiles, and is a little kinder that day than anybody expected. The court physician puts it down to the weather.

choices.text: Let the carving be cold, and see what the king does without encouragement

effects.log: The king looks up at cold wood and looks down again and is no different. That is something to know about a king: what they do when heaven is only paint.

choices.text: Feel, through the wood, who in the hall is lying

effects.log: Three ministers in the front row, and a eunuch behind a pillar. You remember them. From fifteen times a man's height, you will watch them for the rest of their lives.

events.text: Generations of kings. {npc} the carver is long dead; the scaffolding is long gone; the gilt on the carved birds has gone the brown of old honey, and the dancheong around them has been repainted four times. One dawn you fly into the empty hall through a high window and sit on the beam beside your own carving and feel it, very clearly: you could go into the wood now. All of you. And watch every king below for five hundred years.

choices.text: Leave one feather tucked into the carved clouds, and fly out of the window

effects.log: One five-coloured feather, pushed into a crack in the gilt cloud where no sweeper's pole can reach. Then the window, and the morning, and the long sky. The hall keeps the feather. Some day a human life will stand under that ceiling and see it, and not know why they are crying.

choices.text: Fly out of the window. Wood is for things that have finished living

effects.log: You go out into the morning and do not look back. The carvings are only carvings after that. It is a strange thing to lose, and a stranger thing to choose to.

choices.text: Go into the wood with your mate, facing each other among clouds, for good

effects.log: You turn to face your mate on the beam, and the two of you go still, and stiller, and the morning light comes in on two carved birds among gilt clouds, and nothing on the beam that breathes. Below, the court files in. The king on the throne looks up, as kings do.

choices.text: Go into the wood alone, facing the bird the old carver made from a shadow

effects.log: You go into the carving that is you, facing the carving that is whoever {npc} missed most, and you find you do not mind at all. Kings come and go below. One hall, when the others are given dragons, is forgotten, and keeps you both.

events.text: The man who took the throne by night, with the old king's guards bought and the old king's heirs scattered, holds a parade on the day of his crowning. At its head, on a pole, in a gilded cage, rides heaven's sign: a phoenix. It is a cockerel. A very large one, painted in five colours, with a long tail of pheasant feathers glued on, and it is looking at the crowd with the deep, personal anger of a cockerel that has been glued.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Watch from the ridge-tiles, and do not laugh

effects.log: You do not laugh. The crowd does not laugh either: there are soldiers every ten paces. The cockerel crows at noon, very loudly, in the middle of the usurper's speech, and the usurper's face goes the colour of the paint.

choices.text: Look at your mate, and both of you look away very fast

effects.log: You do not laugh until you are five li outside the walls, and then you both laugh so long that a farmer comes out to see what is wrong with the paulownia.

choices.text: Look closer at the paint. Somebody very good did this

effects.log: Mineral blue, cinnabar, a white made of crushed shell, laid on feather by feather by somebody who has studied old paintings of you for years. The glue on the tail is the only lazy thing about it. The painter ran out of time, or of respect.

events.text: You find the painter's lodging behind the dye market by the smell of cinnabar. {npc} is grinding blue in a stone mortar and laughs out loud when you come down to the doorstep in the shape that can speak. "My grandfather's grandfather," {npc} says, "sold a cockerel to a magistrate as a phoenix, in the market at Pyongyang. Got beaten for it. Got the price back twice over. It is the family trade. This usurper is only the biggest customer we ever had."
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: "Stop painting cockerels for usurpers"

ok.log: {npc} grinds the blue a long time. "I will need another trade," {he} says. "Real birds, then. Will you sit?" You will. Slowly, the family business changes.

fail.log: "Easy for you," {npc} says. "You are the real one. Nobody pays the real one." It is unanswerable, and you do not answer it.

choices.text: "Paint the next one worse. Much worse"

mem.note: told me to paint it worse

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit on the floor. The next cockerel has a tail glued on crooked and one blue foot. The court does not notice. The market does, and the joke goes round every wineshop in the capital.

choices.text: Say nothing. Look at the blue in the mortar a long time

effects.log: {npc} stops laughing. "It is the right blue, is it not," {he} says. "I always wondered." You nod. {npc} looks at the mortar as if it had been found out.

events.text: The painted cockerel is dying. The paint was mineral, and the bird has been preening it off for a month and swallowing it, and it sits in its gilded cage on the palace terrace with its eyes half shut. The usurper has already ordered another, and a bigger one, from {npc}.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Open the cage at night and carry the cockerel to a farmyard far away

effects.log: It pecks you twice on the way, out of principle. In a farmyard three valleys off you set it down among hens. It shakes, and a cloud of blue dust comes off it, and it struts away to tell the hens what it has been through. It lives nine more years and is insufferable.

choices.text: Leave it. It is a cockerel, and this is a court

effects.log: It dies in the cage. The usurper has it stuffed. It stands in the throne hall for six years with its glued tail falling off a feather at a time.

choices.text: Sit on the terrace wall beside the cage, in full sight of the guards, for one morning

effects.log: The guards look at the cockerel and then at you and then at the cockerel. By noon the whole palace has seen the real bird sit beside the false one, and nobody can unsee the difference.

events.text: The usurper's first anniversary on the throne, and a second parade, and a second phoenix on a pole, bigger, brighter. The whole capital is lining the road. They are waiting, you realise, to see what the real bird will do. The usurper is waiting too: a ring of archers on the palace roof, with nets.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Fly over the parade, low, in full sight, and on past the palace without stopping

effects.log: You come over the road so low that the crowd feels the wind of your tail. You pass the pole and its cockerel. You pass the palace roof and its archers, and you do not even turn your head. The whole capital watches the phoenix refuse the throne. The usurper lasts two more winters.

choices.text: Land on the palace roof beside the archers and let the court make of it what it will

effects.log: The archers lower their bows; the heralds are out before you have folded your wings. The phoenix has come to the usurper's roof. Heaven favours the reign. It does not, and you know it, and so, in the villages, do the people who learn to spit at banners. (A false omen: -15 purity.)

choices.text: Stay away. Let the people make up their own minds about a cockerel

effects.log: You stay on a far ridge. The cockerel crows in the middle of the speech again. It turns out the people can make up their own minds about a cockerel. It takes them a little longer, that is all.

events.text: The market has a new song. Children sing it skipping rope in the dye-sellers' lane: the chicken king, the chicken king, bought a bird and got a hen. {npc} the painter has been arrested twice and let go twice, because the magistrate's own children sing it. Now {npc} comes out to the city wall at dusk, where you sometimes sit, with a roll of paper under one arm.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Sit for the true painting, as long as {he} needs

mem.note: sat for me on the city wall

effects.log: A season of dusks on the wall. The painting is of one bird under a paulownia at sunrise, and it is good, and in a hundred years it will hang in a hall where kings are crowned, and nobody will know a swindler's family made it.

choices.text: Teach {him} the difference between a cockerel and a phoenix: not the tail, the eyes

effects.log: {npc} looks into your eyes for a long time and then sits down on the wall. "Ah," {he} says. "It is that you are not afraid of anybody." {He} goes home and paints for a year and burns everything, and then paints one good thing.

choices.text: Fly off. A painter has to see the bird leave as well as come

effects.log: You go up off the wall into the dusk. {npc} does not reach for the brush. {He} just watches you go, all the way, until you are a speck, and that is the painting {he} makes: a sky with almost nothing in it.

events.text: An owl sits on the eaves of the Minister of Rites, who has just made himself regent for a king of six: the oldest owl you have ever seen, the colour of bark, holding a rat that has been dead for years. Owls like it have shrieked at you from dead pines since you were a chick, sure you were after what they hold, and this one has the look of having done it longest. When it sees you, it spreads its wings over the rat and screams across the whole palace: "Hsss!"

choices.text: Fly on without a glance

effects.log: You do not look. Behind you the owl screams until it is hoarse. In the regent's rooms the regent hears it and smiles: his bird is warning off his enemies.

choices.text: Land on the opposite roof and look at the owl, and at the rat

effects.log: The rat, this time, is the regency: the seal of a six-year-old king, in the claws of the man who taught the child to bow. The owl sees you looking at it and holds on so hard that its talons go through.

choices.text: Your mate has never met the owl. Introduce them

effects.log: Your mate looks at the owl, and at the rat, and then at you, for a long time. "You have been afraid of THAT," your mate says, "for all these centuries?" You were not afraid. You were. A little.

events.text: The owl comes to your paulownia, which it has never dared to do, and sits on the next branch with the rat held tight. It has learned to talk, in the regent's rooms, and talks fast. "The regent offers you a post," it says. "Court omen. A gilded perch in the throne hall. Sweet water piped from the spring on the hill, which he has walled in for you. The best millet in the kingdom. You will be seen every day. Every day! Is it not what you want? Is it not what you have always wanted?" It hunches over the rat as it says it.

choices.text: "No"

effects.log: The owl does not believe you. It cannot. It goes back to the palace and tells the regent that the phoenix is bargaining.

choices.text: "What is it you are guarding so hard?"

effects.log: The owl looks down at the rat. For a moment, in the moonlight, you think it sees what it is holding. Then it shrieks and flies off, and holds the rat tighter.

choices.text: "Tell the regent the spring on the hill was never his to wall in"

effects.log: The owl takes the message. The regent has the wall round the spring made higher. The spring, which is old and has opinions, goes underground and comes up a mile away in a farmer's field.

events.text: You come down from the eaves at night into the regent's garden in the shape that can speak. The regent, {npc}, is waiting by the walled spring as if it were an appointment, with the owl on {his} shoulder. "I knew you would come in person," {npc} says. "The great always do, in the end. Bless the regency, and the boy will be safe. Refuse, and who knows. Children die so easily."

choices.text: "The boy is not yours to bargain with"

mem.note: defied me in my own garden

effects.log: {npc} smiles. The owl does not. You go up out of the garden, and that night you sit on the roof of the little king's rooms until dawn, where the whole palace can see you. Nobody comes near the child. Not that night.

choices.text: Look at {him} the way the old texts say heaven looks at a ruler, and say nothing at all

effects.log: {npc} holds your eyes as long as anybody ever has. Then {he} looks down at the spring. You leave {him} looking at it.

choices.text: Promise to think about it, to buy the child time

mem.note: said you would think about it

effects.log: A lie, the first you have told a human. It buys the child three years. It costs you something in the breast feathers that does not come back at the next sweet spring. (-3 purity)

events.text: The regent's men come to your paulownia at dawn with a gilded perch carried on poles, and behind it a cage with the door open, and behind that, nets. The owl rides on the gilded perch. It is so excited it has almost let go of its rat. "The post!" it screams. "Take the post! Everyone will see you! Every coronation! For ever!"

choices.text: Say it back to the owl, at last: "Hsss!"

effects.log: "Hsss!" you say, with centuries in it. The owl opens its claws in pure shock, and the rat drops forty feet into the regent's men. Nobody picks it up. The owl looks at its empty claws, and then at you, and for the first time in its life, it has nothing to say.

choices.text: Go up over the nets and away, before the archers string

effects.log: You are up through the leaves and over the ridge before the nets are unrolled. The regent sends hunters after you for nine years. The little king grows up, and one morning has the regent arrested in the garden by the walled spring.

choices.text: Step onto the gilded perch. Let them carry you in

effects.log: You step onto the perch, and it is very comfortable, and the cage door shuts behind it so softly you almost do not hear. Every coronation after that they bring you out to prove heaven's favour, and the people learn to curse two birds on a banner. The owl, at last, has nothing to guard.

events.text: A pilgrim in straw sandals has climbed to the spring where you drink, an old scholar with a book of the classics in {his} pack, and {he} has stopped dead on the path. {npc} is reading you. The old book says the phoenix carries the five virtues written on its body, on the head, the wings, the back, the breast and the belly, and {npc} is looking at you to see which are lit.

choices.text: Turn slowly, so the scholar can read all of you

effects.log: {npc} reads every pattern you have, and counts the dark places where the others will go, and writes it all down that night by a fire. The book goes round three provinces. Kings read it to see which virtue heaven is still waiting for.

choices.text: Drink, and go. You are not a book

effects.log: {npc} sees only a flash of colour and a long tail going up through the pines. {He} writes that the phoenix is modest. You are not. You were thirsty.

choices.text: Ask {him}, in the shape that can speak, which virtue the land below lacks most

effects.log: "Trust," {npc} says at once, and then looks at you, and goes white, because the question was asked by a bird. "Trust," {he} says again, more quietly. "Everyone keeps two ledgers."

events.text: You drink from the spring in the palace garden, as you have since you came in the dance for this reign, and it tastes of iron. Not much. The way water tastes when a nail has been left in the bucket overnight. The ruler you graced is old now, and lately there have been new faces at court, and more men in the prisons than in the granary yards.

choices.text: Drink again, to be sure

effects.log: Iron. No doubt. The reign you blessed is going bad from the root. You have a few years to leave it in sight of everyone, before the pattern it gave you goes dull. (Leave the Land.)

choices.text: Bring your mate to taste it

effects.log: Your mate drinks, and lifts their head, and does not need to say it. You both look at the palace roof where you have perched for years. Neither of you wants to go first. (Leave the Land, in time.)

choices.text: Fly to the sweet spring on the far hill and drink there instead, and think

effects.log: The far spring is clean. That does not make the palace spring sweet again. You sit on the hill and look at the palace for a long time. It is very hard to leave somebody you once blessed. (Leave the Land, while the pattern is still bright.)

events.text: You catch sight of yourself in a still pool and do not at first understand what is wrong. Then you see it: one of your patterns has gone dull, like brass left out in the rain. You stayed too long with a reign gone bad, and it has taken back the thing it gave you.

choices.text: Look at it a long time, and remember the lesson

effects.log: It can be won again, from another worthy reign. That is not the same as never having lost it. You will know, next time, the taste of iron the first day.

choices.text: Fly to the sweet spring at once and wash in it

effects.log: The spring does nothing for the pattern. It does something for you. You come out of the water a little cleaner and no less dull.

choices.text: Let your mate preen the dull place, as if it could be polished

effects.log: It cannot be polished. Your mate does it anyway, all evening, very gently, and you let them. Some things are not done because they work.

events.text: The old ruler's physician, {npc}, comes out into the palace garden at midnight and speaks to the dark under the eaves as if certain that something is listening. "The king dreams of birds," {npc} says. "Every night. Two birds on the roof, and then one, and then none. The king wakes crying that heaven has left. I have no medicine for it. If you are what I think you are, tell me what to give."

choices.text: "Tell the king to open the prisons and the granaries. That is the only medicine"

effects.log: {npc} carries the prescription in, word for word. The king laughs. Then the king does not sleep for a week. Then, one morning, the granary gates are opened, and that night the king sleeps.

choices.text: "There is no medicine for a dream that is true"

effects.log: {npc} bows to the dark. "Then I will give the king something to sleep," {he} says, "and something for myself." You hear {him} weeping on the way back to the gate.

choices.text: Show yourself on the roof at dawn, once, so the king can see you are still there

effects.log: The king sees you from the window and is comforted, and is worse for it, because a king comforted by heaven stops looking at the prisons. You knew that. You came anyway. (-3 purity)

events.text: You are still here. The palace spring has tasted of iron for years, and you are still on the palace roof every morning, because you blessed this reign once and leaving feels like a lie told backwards. A child in the lane below, a water-carrier's child, stops under the eaves with two buckets and looks up at you. "My mother says you are the reason it is all right," the child says. "Is it all right?"

choices.text: Tell the child the truth: no

effects.log: The child nods, as if that was what they thought, and goes on with the buckets. It is the most honest conversation you have had in this capital in a long time. You know what you must do. (Leave the Land.)

choices.text: Say nothing, and look away toward the south

effects.log: The child follows your look south, where the land is green, and puts the buckets down and stands there a while. Children read omens better than courts. (Leave the Land.)

choices.text: Stay one more year. Somebody has to sit here

effects.log: One more year. There is always one more year. The spring tastes of rust now, not iron, and the people in the lane have stopped looking up. (-4 purity)

events.text: From the next ridge you look back at the capital you left. The springs are going. You can see it from here: the palace spring in its carved stone basin is a damp stain, and the wells in the wards are being let down further on longer ropes. The washerwomen at the river have stopped singing. They are looking north, the way you went.

choices.text: Watch one more day, to see what the people do

effects.log: By evening there are lamps lit in a hundred windows that are not usually lit. People are talking. In the morning someone has painted two birds flying north on the wall of the magistrate's office.

choices.text: Turn and fly on, and do not look back again

effects.log: You do not look back. A phoenix that leaves must be seen to leave, and not seen to linger. The capital will read the rest.

choices.text: Your mate looks back. Wait for them

effects.log: Your mate looks back at the city a long time, at the roof you nested on, at the springs going. Then they turn and come, and fly closer to you than usual for a week.

events.text: The capital reads it. In the market a ballad: the phoenixes have gone, the phoenixes have gone, look to the water in the well. The magistrate's men scrub the two painted birds off the office wall; in the morning there are four. Then forty. A child is beaten for drawing one in the dust, and the next day every child in the ward draws one.

choices.text: Sing once, from far off, so they know you heard

effects.log: One long note from the north ridge, at dusk. The whole capital hears it. The magistrate's men stop scrubbing.

choices.text: Keep silent. It is theirs now

effects.log: You say nothing. You do not need to. The people of a capital can read a dry spring and an empty roof faster than any herald can lie about them.

choices.text: Fly over the beaten child's house at dawn, low enough to be seen

effects.log: The child sees you go over and tells the whole ward. The magistrate does not beat any more children. It is not kindness. It is fear of a bird.

events.text: The throne hunts you. Bird-catchers with lime and nets at every paulownia in three provinces; archers on the ridges; a reward of a hundred bolts of silk for the phoenix alive, so it can be made to come back. You are tired, and the store of seed is in a hollow tree two valleys over, and between you and it is a ridge full of nets.

choices.text: Go round the long way, a week of flying hungry

effects.log: A week of mountains and no seed. A phoenix may fly a thousand li hungry. It does not have to enjoy it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go straight over the ridge at dawn, fast and high

ok.log: Over the ridge before the catchers have had their rice. One of them sees you and drops the net and just stares. The reward goes unclaimed another year.

fail.log: A net, half-seen in the mist. You tear through it and leave a long tail feather behind. It is sold to the court for a hundred bolts and presented as proof that the bird is caught. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave the province altogether until the reign is over

effects.log: You go far south, to bamboo country, where nobody has heard of the reward. The reign does not last. Reigns that hunt phoenixes rarely do.

events.text: Sitting low in a pine to rest, you find yourself face to face with one of the hunters: {npc}, a young soldier from a farm village, with a net over one shoulder and an arrow on the string. {He} does not draw. "My mother's spring dried the week you left," {npc} says, very quietly. "Everybody's did. Fly north. The captain is coming up the valley with dogs."

choices.text: "Why are you helping me?"

mem.note: let the phoenix go in the pine

effects.log: "Because if they catch you, the springs will never come back," {npc} says. "Everyone knows that. Even the captain knows that. Go!" You go.

choices.text: "Come back to the farm. The reign will not outlast the dry wells"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the net on {his} shoulder, then drops it in the pine needles. "Desertion," {he} says. "They hang you for it." {He} goes home anyway. You make sure the road home is very quiet.

choices.text: Go without a word

effects.log: You are gone before {npc} can say anything more. That evening the captain's dogs go up the wrong valley. You never learn whether {npc} sent them.

events.text: The reign that hunted you is over. The new ruler of the land does a strange thing in the first spring: has paulownias planted along both sides of the road from the south gate, a hundred of them, and a well dug in every ward, and the prisons emptied of debtors. Nobody is told why. Everybody knows. The springs have not come back yet. The new court is waiting to see if you will.

choices.text: Come back to one of the new paulownias, and only watch

effects.log: You land in the fortieth tree from the gate at dawn. A water-carrier sees you and puts the buckets down and walks home to tell everyone, slowly, so that it is true for longer.

choices.text: Do not come back yet. A good start is only a start

effects.log: You stay away. The new court plants another hundred trees, then digs another hundred wells. Some of the springs come back on their own. That is the right order.

choices.text: Your mate wants to go home. Go home

effects.log: You come back together to the roof you left. The palace spring rises in its stone basin that night, a hand's depth of water that tastes like rice wine. The court weeps. Your mate preens and pretends not to be pleased.

events.text: It happens without your asking. Wherever you settle, the small birds settle: wrens in the hedges, buntings in the millet, magpies on every roof-ridge, a heron on one leg in the paddy. Wherever you leave, they scatter. The old book of rites says it: when the phoenix is kept, the birds do not scatter. A whole valley goes quiet and full when you land, and empty and loud when you go.

choices.text: Settle in one valley a whole year and see what it does

effects.log: A year of full hedges. The caterpillars never reach the cabbages. The farmers have the best harvest in a generation and put it down to the new magistrate, who lets them.

choices.text: Keep moving, so no one valley comes to depend on you

effects.log: You move every season. Behind you the birds settle a little and scatter a little. It is like walking through tall grass: everything bends, nothing breaks.

choices.text: Sing to the birds to see what happens

effects.log: Every bird in the valley sings back at once, a noise like a waterfall made of whistles. A monk in a hermitage falls off a rock. It takes a week for the valley to calm down.

events.text: Two armies in the hills. You are settled in a forest on the ridge between them, and the birds are settled with you, and the scouts of the eastern army have noticed: a forest full of quiet birds is a forest with nobody in it. Except that tonight the western army has sent a thousand men into that forest to lie in wait, and the birds are quiet only because you are there.

choices.text: Leave the forest at dusk, and let the birds rise and warn the scouts

effects.log: You go up, and ten thousand birds go up after you, screaming, out of a forest full of hidden men. The eastern scouts run home. Nobody walks into the ambush. Both armies have dinner, angrily.

choices.text: Stay. It is not your war, and you were here first

effects.log: You stay still, and the birds stay still, and in the morning the eastern army walks up the road into the forest. You leave before the noise starts. You do not go back to that forest for a hundred years. (-2 purity)

choices.text: Sing, so that every bird for ten li rises at once, and nobody can read anything

effects.log: Every forest on both sides of the valley goes up into the sky at once. Neither army can read a thing. Both generals decide heaven is against the battle, and both are right.

events.text: A general finds you. {npc} has followed the birds for a month, because a scout said the phoenix moves with them, and comes up to your paulownia alone and unarmed, and kneels, and speaks to the branch. "Fly with my army," {npc} says. "Where you go the birds go, and where the birds go, the enemy reads that heaven goes. One flight over their camp and they will break without a blow. Think how many lives that saves."

choices.text: "I am not a banner"

mem.note: said you are not a banner

effects.log: {npc} stays kneeling a long time. "No," {he} says at last. "No. I suppose a banner would have said yes." {He} goes back to the army and fights the war the long way.

choices.text: "Ask me again on the day you want peace, not victory"

mem.note: said to ask again for peace

effects.log: {npc} looks up at you for the first time. "That day may come," {he} says. It comes eleven years later, and {npc} asks again, and you fly over both camps, and they go home.

choices.text: Fly once over the enemy camp, as asked

effects.log: The enemy breaks without a blow, as promised. The general's king proclaims heaven's favour on every road, and then on the next war, and the next. You have lent your meaning to an army. (A false omen: -15 purity.)

events.text: The birds hold a council, and it is in your tree, and you are expected to chair it. The magpies want the cranes to stop eating frogs in the magpies' paddies. The cranes say magpies do not eat frogs. The crows want everyone to know that crows were here first. A wren has been talking since dawn, and nobody can remember what about.

choices.text: Rule for the cranes: magpies do not eat frogs

effects.log: The magpies are outraged. They steal every shiny thing in the village in protest. The frogs, who were not consulted, go on as before.

choices.text: Say nothing until they are all quiet. It takes until dusk

effects.log: At dusk, at last, the whole tree is quiet. You say: "Good." Everyone flies home feeling that something has been settled. Nothing has. It is the oldest trick of kings.

choices.text: Let the wren have the last word

effects.log: The wren is so astonished to be allowed to finish that it stops in the middle. Everyone laughs, even the crows. It is the best council the birds of that valley have ever had, and the shortest.

events.text: A southern kingdom of the river plain, with its royal tombs in rows on a hill and its temple between the tombs and the city wall. In the temple's workshop a bronze-caster, {npc}, is making the greatest incense burner ever cast in the kingdom: a dragon for the base, a lotus for the bowl, a lid of mountains where the immortals live, and on the very top, wings spread, a phoenix. {npc} has been working on the phoenix for a year, and it is wrong, and {npc} knows it.

choices.text: Land on the workshop post at dawn and hold still

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the wax and puts down the knife and does not pick it up for an hour. Then {he} scrapes off a year of work and begins again, very fast, without once looking away.

choices.text: Spread your wings once in the temple yard, where {he} can see, and go

effects.log: Once is enough for a great craftsman. {npc} remembers the spread of the wings for the rest of {his} life, the exact angle, the way the tail lifted as the wings opened.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it. A burner is for incense, not for you

effects.log: {npc} finishes the bird from the old paintings. It looks like a duck with ambitions. The king loves it. {npc} never does.

events.text: The wax model is nearly done. Under the bird on the lid sit five musicians, each the size of a fingertip: a flute, a zither on the knees, a drum, a set of pipes, a lute. {npc} carves them with a needle. But the flautist is holding the flute like a stick, and the zither player has the strings the wrong way up, and you have been to a great many courts.

choices.text: Sing the five parts, one by one, while {he} carves each musician

effects.log: {npc} cannot hear music the way you do, but {he} can see a singer breathe. The five tiny musicians come out right: each one leaning into the note. Fourteen centuries later, people will say you can almost hear them.

choices.text: Move the wax flautist's hands yourself, with your beak

effects.log: You bend the soft wax hands round the flute. {npc} stares at the marks of a beak on the model and leaves them there, very small, on the flautist's sleeve. Nobody ever notices.

choices.text: Leave the musicians alone. A bronze-caster is not a court

effects.log: The musicians stay a little wrong, the way real musicians are. It is, perhaps, better. Courts play perfectly. Villages play like this.

events.text: The casting. Clay round the wax, the wax melted out, the bronze poured at night by torchlight with the whole workshop chanting. Then months of chasing and polishing, and then the gold, laid on with mercury and fire until the whole burner shines like the sun coming up behind a mountain. On the top, wings spread, is you. You feel it the way you felt the throne-hall carving: a little of you, gone into the metal.

choices.text: Let it go into the bronze. It is a good place to be

effects.log: When they light the first incense in it, the smoke comes out of the mountains on the lid and climbs past the five musicians, and you, a hundred li away, smell sandalwood on your own feathers.

choices.text: Sit by the furnace and watch it cool, all night

effects.log: You watch until the bronze goes from red to black. {npc} sleeps against the wall with the tongs still in {his} hands. Neither of you is ever going to make anything better than this, and both of you know it.

choices.text: Your mate looks at the bronze bird a long time. "It is one of us," they say. "Which?"

effects.log: You both look at it. It could be either. That is the best thing about it. It is the two of you in one bird, and nobody, ever, will be able to say which half.

events.text: The kingdom's last years. Across the river and over the sea, two great enemies have made common cause. {npc} is old now, and comes to the temple yard every evening to look at the burner in the hall. "When the city falls," {npc} says to the dark under the eaves, "they will melt it for coin. Unless it is not here to find."

choices.text: "The workshop has a water-trough by the furnace vent. Nobody looks in water"

mem.note: told me where to hide it

effects.log: {npc} laughs, an old dry laugh. "In the mud," {he} says. "Yes." {He} goes in to measure the trough, and you sit on the temple roof all night, and both of you are thinking of the same thing: how long mud can keep a secret.

choices.text: "Let it be found and melted. A bird is not its image"

effects.log: {npc} nods, and does not agree, and goes in. You learn, a long time later, that {he} hid it anyway.

choices.text: Sing over the temple at dusk, the five musicians' parts, for the last time

mem.note: sang the five parts for the last time

effects.log: The monks come out into the yard. {npc} stands among them with tears running into {his} beard. Across the river the enemy campfires are lit, a long line of them. Nobody looks at the campfires.

events.text: A small kingdom between two great ones, along a river of iron-smiths. Its king wants a music of its own, so that its people will know who they are while the great kingdoms decide what to do with them. A musician of the court, {npc}, is to make an instrument: a long zither with twelve strings, one for each month. It needs a sound-board of paulownia. {npc} has chosen the tree. It is one of yours.

choices.text: Let the tree go. Fly off the branch so they can cut it

effects.log: You leave the tree at dawn and watch from the next ridge while they cut it, carefully, with a prayer first. {npc} touches the stump afterward the way you touch a friend's shoulder.

choices.text: Stay on the branch until {he} chooses another tree

effects.log: {npc} sees you, and puts the axe down, and stands under the tree a long time. Then {he} goes and cuts a younger one, on the far side of the hill. The zither sounds a little thin, ever after. Thin and true.

choices.text: Show {him} an old paulownia that fell in last year's storm, seasoned and sound

effects.log: {npc} follows you through the woods all morning, half-afraid, to a fallen giant in the ferns. {He} knocks on it and listens, and then sits down on it and laughs. "A year dried already," {he} says. "Heaven sends wood."

events.text: {npc} has made the zither: long as a person, twelve silk strings on twelve wooden bridges like a line of geese. {He} sits under your tree at dusk to tune it and cannot get the middle strings to agree with each other. Every evening, a little worse. {He} has been asked to write twelve songs for twelve villages, and the strings will not settle.

choices.text: Sing the note from the branch, once

effects.log: {npc} stops, and turns the peg, and plucks, and it is your note. {He} tunes the other eleven strings to it by moonlight. The twelve songs come in a year: one for each village, named for them, and every one starts on your note.

choices.text: Sing nothing. Let {him} find it

effects.log: It takes {npc} three more months, and {he} finds it, and it is not quite your note, and it is {his}, and the songs are better for it.

choices.text: Sing the note with your mate, so it comes as a chord

effects.log: Two notes, a fifth apart, from one tree. {npc} tunes to both, and the zither has a sound no other zither has, as if two people were playing. Every village says so.

events.text: The small kingdom falls, as small kingdoms between great ones do. {npc} is on the road north toward the conqueror's capital with the zither on {his} back, and stops at a ford where you are drinking, and speaks to you in the dusk as if to an old colleague. "They say I am a traitor," {npc} says, "to carry our music to the king who took our land. Is music a traitor? Tell me. You have sat over enough thrones."

choices.text: "Music that is kept in a burned house is ash. Carry it"

mem.note: told me to carry the music

effects.log: {npc} sits a long time at the ford. Then {he} stands, and settles the zither on {his} back, and goes north. The twelve songs go with {him}, with the names of twelve villages that no longer have a king.

choices.text: "Music has no country. Only players do"

effects.log: "Then I am the traitor and the music is innocent," {npc} says. "That is easier. Thank you." {He} goes north, lighter.

choices.text: "I do not know"

mem.note: even the phoenix did not know

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud. "Even you," {he} says. "Good. Then nobody does, and I can stop asking." {He} plays one song at the ford, the one for the village by the river, and goes on.

events.text: In the conqueror's court three young musicians have studied under {npc} for years, and now they play their master the twelve songs as they have rearranged them: cut down to five, the slow parts gone, the village names changed. {npc} is old and furious and sits through all five with a face like a shut door. You are on the roof. You can hear every note.

choices.text: Sing along with the new version, very softly

effects.log: Halfway through the fourth song {npc} hears a voice on the roof joining in, and stops scowling, and listens differently. At the end {he} says: "Joyful, and not wanton. Yes. Play it like that." The court writes it down.

choices.text: Sing the old version, all twelve, from the roof, that night

effects.log: All twelve, slow parts and village names, into the conqueror's night. {npc} sits up in bed and listens to the end. In the morning {he} is gentler with the students. The old songs have been heard once more. That is enough.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is the teacher's to decide

effects.log: {npc} decides, after a week, that the five are good. It is the hardest thing {he} has ever done, harder than the road north. The music goes on, changed, and outlives the conquerors too.

events.text: Word comes the way word comes to you, from bird to bird: on an island off the south coast an old scholar in exile has planted a paulownia by a hut, and sits under it every morning, and says aloud, to nobody: "The phoenix does not come. The river gives no chart. I am finished." It is what the sage said in the old book, when the world went wrong. You were in another land, watching another court.

choices.text: Go now, across the sea

effects.log: Two days over grey water. Gulls laugh at you the whole way. You arrive with salt in your feathers and your heart going like a drum. (-5 health)

choices.text: Finish what you are doing here first. A year, no more

effects.log: You finish watching the court. It takes a year. It takes a little more than a year.

choices.text: Send your mate ahead while you finish here

effects.log: Your mate goes ahead, and does not like going alone, and says so for a hundred li. You follow a season later. It is the first time in centuries you have flown apart.

events.text: The island. A thatched hut, a garden of radishes, a paulownia the height of two people, and under it, at dawn, {npc}: very old, very thin, in a scholar's robe gone to rags, with a book face down on {his} knee. {He} is looking out to sea and saying it again, the old words, as if they were a prayer that had stopped working. Then {he} looks up.

choices.text: Land in the paulownia, and stay all morning

effects.log: {npc} does not move. Tears go down into {his} beard and {he} does not wipe them. At noon {he} says: "Then I am not finished." {He} lives four more years, and writes in every one of them.

choices.text: Come down in the shape that can speak, and sit beside {him}

mem.note: sat with me, a stranger with five-coloured eyes

effects.log: You talk all day, about the old books and the new kings. {npc} knows exactly what you are by the second hour and is too well-mannered to say so. When you leave, {he} bows to your back.

choices.text: Your mate is already here, in the tree. Join them

effects.log: Your mate has been sitting in the paulownia for a season, and the old scholar has been talking to them every morning, and now there are two. {npc} laughs out loud. "Two," {he} says. "Of course. The books always said two."

events.text: You come to the island too late. The hut is shut, the radishes have bolted, and under the paulownia there is a new grave, a low mound with a plain stone. The island children say the old scholar died in the spring, sitting under the tree, still looking out to sea. The last words were the ones from the old book. A missed sage.

choices.text: Sit on the grave tree every dawn for a year

effects.log: A year of dawns on the island. The children come to look at you, then the fishermen, then the whole island. They put the scholar's book under the tree in a box. It is too late for the scholar. It is not too late for the island.

choices.text: Sing over the grave once, the whole of your song, and go

effects.log: You sing it all, both halves, over the low mound. Then you go back across the sea. You will carry this one. Some birds carry stones in their crops to grind their food. This is like that.

choices.text: Your mate says nothing. That is worse

effects.log: Your mate sits on the gravestone and does not look at you all morning. It was your year, your court, your choice. You both know it. You fly home closer than usual anyway.

events.text: The paulownia on the island has grown. The scholar's students, grey-haired now, have built a little schoolhouse beside it with a roof of reeds, and teach the island's children to read from the scholar's own books. A small girl recites the old words, the phoenix does not come, and the teacher stops her and says: "It came. Read the next line we wrote."

choices.text: Perch on the schoolhouse roof while the lesson goes on

effects.log: The lesson does not go on. Nobody could expect it to. The teacher gives up and lets the children come out and look, and it is the best lesson that schoolhouse ever has.

choices.text: Leave a feather in the paulownia for the teacher to find

effects.log: The teacher finds it in the morning and does not tell anyone for a month. Then it is in a box on the schoolhouse shelf, beside the scholar's book, and every child on the island has seen it.

choices.text: Watch from a distance. It is theirs

effects.log: You sit on the far headland and listen to children reading in the wind. You stay longer than you mean to. You always do.

events.text: One dawn, singing on the ridge, you hear something new come out of your own throat: the five notes of the old scale all at once, gung and sang and gak and chi and u, each of them clear, none of them crowding the others. The valley goes quiet. A waterfall, you would swear, misses a beat.

choices.text: Sing it again, to be sure it is yours

effects.log: It is yours. Five notes, one voice. A court musician on the road below sits down in the dust with his zither across his knees and does not get up until noon.

choices.text: Stop at once. A voice like that is a responsibility

effects.log: You sing nothing for a month and think. What a voice like that can do to a quarrel, a sickroom, a battle. It is not a toy. It is not even a gift. It is a weight.

choices.text: Sing it to your mate, and see whether they can answer in five

effects.log: Your mate answers in three, then four, then, on the fifth morning, in five, and the two of you sing ten notes together on the ridge and frighten every bird for a hundred li.

events.text: A walled town under siege, the forty-first day. The besiegers have a ring of fires round it, and the defenders have thrown their last arrows and are pulling up flagstones to throw instead. Tomorrow the walls go. You are on a cliff above the valley at dusk, and both sides are close enough to hear you.

choices.text: Sing the five notes over both armies

effects.log: The besiegers stop hammering. The defenders stop prying at stones. On both sides, men sit down where they stand. Nobody gives an order. All night, nobody fights. In the morning nobody can remember quite how to start.

choices.text: Sing only over the town, for the people inside

effects.log: Inside the walls, a night of sleep, the first in forty days. In the morning the defenders fight like people who have slept. The siege goes on a month more and then breaks, both ways.

choices.text: Do not sing. A truce sung by a bird is not a truce

effects.log: You keep silent. In the morning the walls go, and the town is taken, and it is not as bad as it might have been, and it is bad. You will not know, ever, what the song would have done.

events.text: After the night of the song, the besieging commander, {npc}, walks out alone to the foot of your cliff without armour and calls up to you, quite politely, as if to a magistrate on a high bench. "I have forty days in this valley," {npc} says, "and two thousand men who will not fight. You did that. So. What do you suggest?"

choices.text: "Go to the gate and ask for water. They have been thirsty longer than you"

mem.note: told me to ask for water

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, then laughs, then goes. The gate opens a crack for {him}. By noon the two commanders are sitting on a cart in the middle of the field drinking from one gourd.

choices.text: "I suggest nothing. I sang. The rest is yours"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "That is fair," {he} says. "Unhelpful, but fair." {He} goes back to camp and thinks all day, and does not attack.

choices.text: "Go home before the song wears off"

effects.log: {npc} goes home. Half the army goes with {him}, and half stays, and the half that stays fights a smaller, sadder siege, and loses.

events.text: The truce of one night has held, and become a truce of seasons. Now the two lords have agreed to meet under your paulownia to make it a truce of one year, and both of them have brought far too many guards, and every guard's hand is on a sword. They are waiting for you to sing. You realise that if you sing, they will sign; and that if you ever stop singing, they will draw.

choices.text: Sing, and let them sign

effects.log: They sign. The year holds. So does the next, a little less. A peace that needs a bird to sing it is a peace on a branch. (-2 purity)

choices.text: Stay silent, and make them sign without the song

ok.log: They wait for the song. It does not come. The silence goes on so long that one of the lords, out of pure embarrassment, picks up the brush and signs, and the other cannot be seen not to. It holds for years.

fail.log: The silence is too long. A guard coughs, a hand moves, steel shows. You sing, quickly, before anyone is killed, and they sign. It holds four years.

choices.text: Fly off before they arrive. Let them meet under an empty tree

effects.log: They arrive at an empty tree and stand there feeling foolish, and that, in the end, is what makes them talk to each other.

events.text: An envoy from the empire of the plains has come to the vassal king of the land below with a list. Ginseng, paper, horses, falcons, silk. And, in the emperor's own hand at the bottom: a pair of the five-coloured birds of the east, living, since the emperor has heard that the east has phoenixes and the empire does not. The vassal king reads the list in the throne hall, and looks up at the ceiling for a long time.

choices.text: Watch from the roof, and see what the king does

effects.log: The king sends the envoy away with ginseng and horses and promises. Then the king calls in the bird-catchers, and sits with them a long time with the doors shut.

choices.text: Take your mate far south at once

effects.log: You go south the same night, to bamboo country, and lie low for a season. It is not far enough. Empires have long lists and longer memories.

choices.text: Leave a long feather in the throne hall, as if to say: this is all you will get

effects.log: The king finds it on the dais and holds it a long time, and sends it to the empire with a letter. The empire is not satisfied. The empire is never satisfied.

events.text: The vassal king, {npc}, comes alone to the foot of your paulownia at night and speaks upward in a low, steady voice, as kings learn to speak. "The emperor's armies are on the river," {npc} says. "The envoy says: two phoenixes, or ten thousand soldiers. I have counted my soldiers. I am asking you. One year in the emperor's garden. I will beg for you to be sent home. I do not know if they will listen."

choices.text: "No. Find another way, or fight"

effects.log: {npc} bows, and goes. Three nights later the bird-catchers come anyway, with lime and nets, on the king's orders or the envoy's. You never find out which.

choices.text: "Send the envoy to me. I will speak to the empire myself"

effects.log: The envoy comes, and you speak, and the envoy writes it all down and does not believe a word, and three nights later the nets come anyway. The empire does not take dictation from tribute.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go higher into the mountains

effects.log: You go higher. {npc} sits under the empty tree until dawn. The nets come up the mountain after you, slowly, the way water climbs a rope.

events.text: Night, and nets. They come over the paulownia from three sides at once, weighted with stones, and you are out through a gap and into the sky before you understand. Your mate is not. You hear them: tangled, beating, calling your half of the song. Torches. Men with poles. A cage on a cart, with a red cloth ready.

choices.text: Dive back into the net and tear it open

ok.log: You come down through the torches with your claws first. Silk cord parts, a pole breaks, a catcher runs. Your mate comes up out of the net behind you, and the two of you are over the ridge before the cage is even unlocked. (-15 health)

fail.log: You tear one net and a second comes down over the first. Your mate shouts at you to go. You go, because they shouted, and from the ridge you watch the red cloth go over the cage. (-20 health)

choices.text: Follow the cart. Wherever they take your mate, you go

effects.log: The cart goes north under the red cloth. You go north above it, out of bowshot, every day, every night. Your mate can hear you. You make sure of it.

choices.text: Sing over the catchers until they cannot bear to go on

effects.log: Two of the catchers drop their poles and walk away weeping. Four do not. The red cloth goes over the cage. Somewhere under it, very quietly, your mate is singing their half back.

events.text: The emperor's capital: a city of walls inside walls, and in the innermost, a garden where the empire keeps the tribute of the world. Elephants, a striped horse, a long-necked spotted beast that eats from the treetops. And in a gilded cage under a willow, your mate, thinner, with their tail feathers pulled for the empress's fan. They see you on the wall. They do not call. They know better.

choices.text: Wait for the night of the lantern festival and break the cage

ok.log: Ten thousand lanterns, and every guard looking up at them, and nobody looking at a willow. The cage door is only wire. You are over the walls before the next lantern is lit, two of you, and nobody in that city ever admits the phoenixes were there at all. (-10 health)

fail.log: A guard is looking at the willow after all. Arrows. You go up over the wall with one in your wing. Your mate watches you go, and puts their head under their wing, and waits. (-20 health)

choices.text: Sing outside the walls every dawn until the empire grows tired of the noise

effects.log: You sing every dawn for a year. The empress cannot sleep. The emperor's mother says it is a curse. In the second spring a eunuch is sent to open the cage and look the other way.

choices.text: Go home alone. The empire is too big

effects.log: You fly home across the plains alone. On the first dawn back on the ridge you sing both halves of the song, badly. The mountains still answer with two. You wish they would not.

events.text: In the inner quarters of the palace the queen, {npc}, sits up at night with a long gold hairpin in {his} hands, the kind with a phoenix on its head, worn for ceremonies. You are on the ridge of the roof. {npc} speaks to the hairpin, quietly, as if it could hear, and then lifts {his} head and looks straight at the dark where you are. "If you are what this is made of," {npc} says, "come down. I need help, and there is no one else I trust."

choices.text: Come down the eaves to the courtyard in the shape that can speak

effects.log: {npc} does not scream, or bow. {He} pours tea for two and says: "They mean to poison my son before the new year. I know who. I cannot prove it. And I am only the queen."

choices.text: Stay on the roof, but answer

effects.log: "Thank you," {npc} says to the dark. "Then listen. They mean to poison my son before the new year." You listen until the lantern burns down.

events.text: The plot is ordinary, as plots go: the old king's favourite consort, a brother at the Board of War, a cook in the crown prince's kitchen paid in land. {npc} has laid it all out for you on a tray in the lamplight, with the hairpin beside it. "I do not ask you to kill anybody," {npc} says. "I know what you are not. I ask you: what can a phoenix do, that a queen cannot?"

choices.text: "I can be seen. Let me be seen on the roof of the prince's kitchen"

effects.log: Every morning for a month there is a phoenix on the ridge of the prince's kitchen. The cook goes grey and resigns. The brother at the Board of War catches a sudden illness and goes to the hot springs. Nobody is accused of anything. Nothing happens. That was the point.

choices.text: "I am not a guard. But I will tell you which dishes smell of iron"

effects.log: You sit on the kitchen roof at every meal for a season and send a sparrow down when a dish smells wrong. Three dishes are spilled by a clumsy maid on {npc}'s orders. The prince grows up very fond of plain rice.

choices.text: "Nothing. A phoenix that takes sides in a palace stops being a phoenix"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the hairpin for a long time and then puts it in {his} hair. "Then I shall have to be a phoenix myself," {he} says. You are not sure, afterward, that you were right.

events.text: Years later. The prince is king, and {npc} is the queen dowager, and comes out alone on the night of the first snow to the courtyard with the hairpin, and lays it on the stone step. "I never wore it again," {npc} says to the roof. "After that winter, it felt like wearing a friend. I would like you to have it back."

choices.text: Take it, gently, in your beak, and carry it to your paulownia

effects.log: It sits in the fork of your tree for two hundred years, gold going green, until the tree grows round it. Somewhere in the wood of a very old paulownia there is a queen's hairpin. Someday a zither-maker will find it, and be very surprised.

choices.text: Push it back to {him} with your beak. "Give it to your granddaughter. That one will need it"

mem.note: told me to pass the pin on

effects.log: {npc} laughs in the snow, the first time you have ever heard {him} laugh. "That one will," {he} says. "That one is just like me." The pin goes down the generations, with a story attached, and the story is mostly true.

events.text: Summer comes north early, and too hot, and on the third night of it a column of sparks stands up over the southern ridge as tall as a mountain. It comes toward you. The heat arrives first: the paulownia leaves curl, the spring steams. Then a voice out of the sparks, delighted, enormous: "Cousin! Cousin of the south! I have looked for you for five hundred years!" It is the Vermilion Bird, the guardian of the south. It thinks you are its kin.

choices.text: Greet it politely, from a distance

effects.log: You bow on the branch. The column of sparks bows back, and three of your leaves catch fire. It apologises very warmly, which does not help.

choices.text: Ask it, gently, to stand back from your trees

effects.log: It stands back. A little. The heat goes from unbearable to only very hot. "Of course," it says. "Of course. You have always been the delicate one."

choices.text: Your mate puts themself between the heat and the nest

effects.log: Your mate spreads their wings over the nest and stares into the sparks without blinking. The Vermilion Bird is impressed. "Fierce," it says. "Good. Our family has always been fierce." (-5 health)

events.text: The Vermilion Bird stays a season, and the season is the hottest anyone remembers. It is generous with everything: stories of the south wall of the sky, of the summer it holds, of the fires it has started for good reasons. And everywhere it perches, your paulownias scorch. Two of them die standing. The farmers below have begun to call this the burning summer.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is a guest, and it is lonely

effects.log: You say nothing. Another tree dies. The Vermilion Bird tells you about every one of the five hundred years it looked for you, and you understand that nobody in all that time has let it finish a sentence.

choices.text: Take it to the high bare ridges where nothing burns

effects.log: You lead it up to bare rock above the treeline, and it settles there like a forge, and talks, and the valleys below cool by a little. It does not notice what you did. You do not tell it.

choices.text: Tell it plainly that it is killing your trees

effects.log: The column of sparks goes very still. "Oh," it says. It moves to the river and sits in the shallows in a cloud of steam for a week, sulking, and not one more tree dies.

events.text: The Vermilion Bird asks you to burn with it. Just once. "Open your wings to the fire," it says, "and you will remember what you are. You are the bird that burns and is not consumed. You are the summer. You are me." The heat of it is so close now that your tail feathers smell of smoke.

choices.text: "I am not you. I am wood, and the music made of wood"

effects.log: The sparks waver. "Wood," it says, as if tasting the word. "Wood burns." "Yes," you say. "That is why I do not stand near fire." It looks at you a long time. "Then we are not family," it says, and it sounds very young.

choices.text: "We are both birds of heaven. That is enough family"

effects.log: The Vermilion Bird thinks about it, flickering. "Cousins," it says at last. "Not sisters, not brothers. Cousins." It sounds pleased. It sounds as if it has never had a cousin.

choices.text: Open one wing to the heat, a little, to understand it

effects.log: It is like putting your wing into the sun. Three feathers blacken and drop. You understand, for one instant, what it is to be summer, and you never want to again. (-15 health)

events.text: The autumn wind comes, and the Vermilion Bird must go south to hold its wall. It stands over the ridge, a little smaller than it came, the sparks a little slower. "Will I see you again, phoenix?" it says. "Or was this a mistake?"

choices.text: "Come north every thousand years, and stand on the bare ridge"

effects.log: "A thousand years," it says. "That is nothing. That is a summer." It goes south as a long red line of sparks over the mountains, and every thousand years after, the hottest summer comes, and stays on the bare ridges, and does not burn the trees.

choices.text: "It was a mistake. Do not come back"

effects.log: The sparks go out, all at once, and come back dimmer. It goes south without a word. Twice in the next century there are fires in your groves that nobody can explain. You know who it was. It was very, very hurt.

choices.text: Your mate answers for both of you: "Go well, cousin"

effects.log: The Vermilion Bird hears two voices, and is startled, and then very glad. "Two," it says, "two cousins," and goes south singing, so loud that the whole southern sky goes red at dusk for a week.

events.text: On the post outside every teahouse in the martial world, a new list: the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, the most promising fighters under thirty. You land on the teahouse roof one morning to listen to the young ones argue about it, and realise, slowly, that they are using your name. They have been using it for generations. Not one of them has ever seen you.

choices.text: Listen all morning to who they think deserves it

effects.log: They argue about swords, speed, sects, who beat whom in which spring tournament. Not one of them mentions whether anybody on the list is kind. You think about that all the way home.

choices.text: Let your shadow fall across the list, once

effects.log: A long shadow with a long tail slides across the posted list at noon. Thirty young fighters look up at once, and see nothing but the sun. By evening the story is in every teahouse in three provinces.

choices.text: Fly on. A name is not a debt

effects.log: You fly on. The young ones go on arguing. They will be arguing in five hundred years.

events.text: A young swordsman, {npc}, ninth on the list of Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, has climbed your mountain for a week with a bundle of rice and a sword, looking for you. When you come down in the shape that can speak, {npc} knows at once, and bows so low {his} topknot touches the rock. "I wanted to see a real one," {npc} says. "Before I fight for the eighth place. So I would know what the name was supposed to mean."

choices.text: "It means: be worth seeing"

mem.note: told me to be worth seeing

effects.log: {npc} repeats it all the way down the mountain. {He} loses the fight for eighth place, and spares the winner a humiliation {he} could have handed out, and is the only fighter on the list that year anyone remembers kindly.

choices.text: Show {him}: rise into your true shape on the morning light

mem.note: saw the real phoenix rise at dawn

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the rock with {his} mouth open and stays there until noon. {He} does not try for eighth place that year, or any year. {He} goes home and teaches children.

choices.text: "Go home. The name is a trap they set for the young"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you as if you had struck {him}. Then, slowly, {he} begins to laugh. "Yes," {he} says. "It is, is it not." {He} fights for eighth place anyway, and wins, and never takes the list seriously again.

events.text: A morning of clear sky, and across the whole east of it a long coil of white cloud lifts and turns, very slowly, the way a great sleeping thing turns over, and lowers one end toward your ridge, like a head nodding. If the world has an Azure Dragon, this is how it greets a phoenix: from the far side of the sky, without coming any closer, as the two names have always sat in the young ones' list, side by side and never touching.

choices.text: Answer with one long note across the sky

effects.log: The note goes out over three provinces. The coil of cloud holds still a long moment, and then turns back over, and is only cloud. Below, in every training ground in the east, young fighters stop and look up and do not know why.

choices.text: Bow on the branch, and keep silent

effects.log: You bow. The cloud dissolves into ordinary weather. Some greetings are better answered by being understood.

choices.text: Rise with your mate and fly a circle under the cloud

effects.log: Two birds circle under the coil of cloud, and the cloud, very slightly, circles too. The farmers below see it and plant early that year, and have the best harvest in a generation.

events.text: Many years on, {npc} is grey, and the master of a training ground on the mountain where you first met, and on the morning before the great tournament the young ones of the list come up in a crowd to look at the paulownia where the phoenix is said to sit. You are sitting in it. And you feel, very clearly, that you could give yourself to them: become the name, the dawn before every first great fight, for every generation after this one.

choices.text: Bless only the one who planted this whole story: land on {npc}'s shoulder, once

mem.note: landed on my shoulder in front of everyone

effects.log: The crowd goes silent. {npc} stands very still with a phoenix on {his} shoulder and weeps in front of every young fighter in the east. Then you go. The young ones remember it all their lives, and it is not the bird they remember.
