choices.text: Fly off before anyone sees you. The name is theirs, not yours

effects.log: You are gone before the crowd reaches the top of the path. They find an empty tree, and one of them, the youngest, says it does not matter: they will just have to deserve it anyway. {npc} hears, and smiles.

choices.text: Give yourself to the young. Become the name

effects.log: You rise on the morning light over the crowd of young faces and do not come down. From then on, in every generation, the most promising are called the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, and the best of them, on the morning of their first great fight, see two birds at dawn.

events.text: {npc}, to whom you gave a feather, has been a magistrate for one month. On the second evening of the second month a rice merchant comes to the county office with a lacquered box, and sets it down on the desk, and goes, and the box is heavy. {npc} sits looking at it with one hand inside {his} sleeve, where the feather is.

choices.text: Do nothing. It is their test, not yours

ok.log: {npc} sends the box back unopened with a note so polite it is almost an insult. The merchant tells everyone. Within a year no one in the county tries again.

fail.log: {npc} opens the box. Closes it. Opens it again. In the end {he} sends it back, but only half, and you feel the other half in your breast feathers for a week. (-2 purity)

choices.text: Let the feather go warm in {his} sleeve

mem.note: warmed the feather in my sleeve

effects.log: {npc} feels it, the warmth, like a hand on the arm. {He} sends the box back, and sits a long time afterward with the feather out on the desk, looking at it as if it had spoken.

choices.text: Sit on the office wall where {he} can see you through the window

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the box and sees you on the wall, and laughs out loud, alone in the office. The box goes back. You are not sure whether you helped or cheated.

events.text: A flood year in {npc}'s county. The rice is under brown water to the knee, and the government granary is full, and the granary may only be opened on an order from the capital, ten days away by road. {npc} stands at the granary gate in the rain with the key in one hand and the other in {his} sleeve. The crowd at the gate is very quiet.

choices.text: Fly over the granary in full sight of the crowd

effects.log: The crowd sees the phoenix go over the granary roof and looks at {npc}. {npc} opens the gate. When the order from the capital comes, a month later, it is a reprimand, and it is framed, and it hangs in the county office for three hundred years.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let {him} choose with no sign at all

effects.log: {npc} stands at the gate until dark. Then {he} opens it, slowly, with no sign from heaven at all, which is the only kind of courage that counts. You were very proud. You did not let {him} see.

choices.text: Sing over the flood until the water goes down a little

effects.log: You sing three days in the rain. The water goes down a hand's width, which is something. {npc} opens the granary on the fourth day anyway, and is reprimanded anyway. (-5 health)

events.text: {npc} has risen. A governor now, and the test is bigger: the son of the greatest family in the province has beaten a servant to death, and the family has sent word, very politely, that a governor's career is a fragile thing. The case is on {npc}'s desk. So is {his} hand, and in {his} hand, turning, the feather.

choices.text: Trust {him}. Do nothing

ok.log: {npc} tries the son in open court and sentences the son by the law, and is dismissed within the year, and goes home to a small house with a paulownia, and is never sorry. You go and sit in the tree.

fail.log: {npc} lets the case be lost. A clerk, a missing witness, a fever. The family is grateful. The feather in {his} sleeve goes cold, and so, a little, does something in your breast. You will feel it again, every decade, for as long as {npc} lives.

choices.text: Come to {him} at night, in the shape that can speak, and say only: "I am watching"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Yes," {he} says. "That is what I was afraid of. And hoping for." The son is tried. {npc} is dismissed. You both think it was cheap at the price.

choices.text: Take the feather back

effects.log: You come in through the window at midnight and take it from the desk. {npc} watches you do it and does not stop you, and you never learn what {he} would have done. Some tests are better not finished.

events.text: {npc} is very old, and dying in a small house with a paulownia over the roof, and asks to be carried out into the yard to see the morning. You are in the tree. {He} holds up the feather, faded now, the colours gone to the browns of an old painting. "I did my best with it," {npc} says. "Not always. Mostly. What do I do with it now?"

choices.text: "Give it to whoever in your family is most afraid of being tested"

effects.log: A grandchild, a shy one, is called out of the house and given the feather and does not know what to do with their hands. {npc} dies smiling at the face the child makes. The feather goes on, down the generations, faded and kept.

choices.text: Come down and take it, and stay with {him} to the end

effects.npcPass: old age, with the phoenix in the yard
effects.log: You come down into the yard and take the feather back in your beak, and {npc} puts a hand on your neck, and leaves it there, and goes, quite peacefully, before the sun is fully up.

choices.text: "Bury it with you. You earned it"

effects.log: It goes into the ground with {npc}, in the hand, under the tree. Some human life, some day, will dig there and find a faded feather in an old magistrate's grave, and understand nothing, and keep it anyway.

events.text: Water is coming up between the flagstones of the palace courtyard: clear, cold, a little spring the size of a rice bowl, bubbling in the crack between two stones in front of the throne hall. The ministers stand round it in their robes. Half of them say it is heaven's favour on the reign: a sweet spring rises in a just land. The other half say it is a broken pipe.
events.arc: The Spring in the Palace Courtyard

choices.text: Drink from it in full sight, at dawn

effects.log: You come down on the flagstones in the grey light and drink. The ministers who said it was heaven's favour go pale with joy. The ministers who said it was a pipe go pale with something else.

choices.text: Taste it secretly at night

effects.log: You come down when the courtyard is empty and taste it. It is very good water. It is also, faintly, the taste of the clay pipe that runs under the courtyard from the hill. Both things are true.

choices.text: Stay away. A spring argued over by ministers is not a spring

effects.log: You stay on the hill. The ministers argue for a year and build a little stone wall round the crack and appoint an official to guard it. The official is the only person who drinks from it, and grows very healthy.

events.text: The court engineers dig up the flagstones to settle the question. Under them, as the doubters said, an old clay pipe from the hill, cracked. But the hill spring that feeds the pipe dried up forty years ago, under the last reign, and nobody can say where this water is coming from.
events.arc: The Spring in the Palace Courtyard

choices.text: Fly up to the hill and look for yourself

effects.log: The old hill spring is running again, quietly, under the moss, for the first time in a long while. Nobody went up to look. Nobody thought to. A just land does not always announce itself; sometimes it just leaks.

choices.text: Let it be a mystery

effects.log: It stays a mystery. The engineers lay the stones back. The water keeps coming. It is, you think, the best kind of omen: one that might be plumbing.

events.text: A young official, {npc}, put in charge of the little spring because nobody else wanted the post, comes out at dusk and sits on the edge of the stone wall round it and talks to the water, because there is nobody else to talk to. When you come down in the shape that can speak and sit on the other side, {npc} is not even surprised. "Is it heaven," {npc} asks, "or a pipe? I have to write a report."
events.arc: The Spring in the Palace Courtyard

choices.text: "Write: both"

effects.log: {npc} writes it: the spring is heaven's and the pipe's. The report is laughed at in the capital, then quoted, then made into a proverb, and {npc} is promoted for wit.

choices.text: "Write that a just land keeps its pipes mended"

mem.note: told me a just land keeps its pipes mended

effects.log: {npc} writes it, and the court reads it, and somebody very senior is annoyed enough to order every pipe in the capital mended. It is the most useful report of the reign.

choices.text: Drink from the spring and leave without a word

mem.note: saw the phoenix drink at the courtyard spring

effects.log: {npc} watches you go, and writes the shortest report in the history of the court: "The phoenix drank." Nobody argues with it again.

events.text: The egg. You had forgotten what it was like: the colour of a coal that has stopped burning, the warmth that comes from inside it and not from you. The last egg of your kind was your own, in the red sand of a cave, with nobody sitting on it. This one has two of you. You take turns. Neither of you sleeps much.

choices.text: Take the long night watches yourself

effects.log: You sit through the long nights and your mate through the short days. Your mate pretends not to notice that you have taken the hard half. You pretend not to notice them noticing. (-5 health)

choices.text: Sing to it, softly, both halves of the song

effects.log: Something in the egg goes still when you sing, and then knocks, once, from inside, when you stop. Your mate laughs, a sound you have not heard from them in a century.

choices.text: Watch the ground below for anyone who has heard

effects.log: A woodcutter. A monk. Two men who do not look like either, and who look up at your tree a little too long. You remember their faces.

events.text: The two men who looked up too long come back with a third: {npc}, an alchemist of a sect in the south mountains, with a pack full of jars. {He} stands under the paulownia and speaks upward, reasonably. "An elixir of a phoenix egg is said to add five hundred years," {npc} says. "I can pay in anything you like. Sweet springs. Groves of bamboo. A mountain with no hunters on it. Name it."

choices.text: Come down in the shape that can speak and look {him} in the eye until {he} goes

effects.log: {npc} holds your look longer than most, and then not as long as {he} needs to. The three of them go down the mountain together without speaking. The jars clink all the way.

choices.text: Sing the five notes at {him} until {his} breath will not settle

effects.log: {npc} sits down in the snow, then lies down, gasping, and {his} men carry {him} off. You have never used your voice as a weapon before. You do not like what it felt like. (-5 health)

choices.text: Move the egg, at night, to another tree

ok.log: A whole night of moving an egg in the snow, a branch at a time, the two of you, terrified. By dawn it is in a paulownia two valleys off. The alchemist climbs to an empty nest.

fail.log: The alchemist's men were watching. A net in the dark, a fight on a frozen branch. You keep the egg. You leave feathers and blood on the snow. (-15 health)

events.text: It hatches at dawn. It is drab, and damp, and the size of a sparrow, and very, very loud. It tumbles out of the shell, looks at nothing in particular, and at once begins to sing and to dance by itself, to nobody, wings out, falling over, getting up, singing. It does not look at you. It does not need to.

choices.text: Laugh

effects.log: You laugh, and your mate laughs, and the chick takes no notice whatever and sings louder. You were exactly like this. Your mate says so. You deny it.

choices.text: Dance with it

effects.log: You dance on the branch beside it, very carefully, three steps of the measured dance. The chick looks at you, for the first time, with deep disapproval, and does its own steps instead.

choices.text: Just watch

effects.log: You watch all morning. You have watched kings and armies and the springs of whole kingdoms. Nothing has ever been as interesting as this.

events.text: The chick will not eat millet. A sparrow offers it some, kindly, and it turns its head away. It will eat only the seed you bring from the bamboo, and drink only from the spring you show it, and sleep only in the paulownia. It is, you realise, going to be exactly as difficult as you were. It also eats a great deal.

choices.text: Share your store with it

effects.log: The store goes down faster than you expected. Chicks eat. You eat less. Nobody complains, except the chick, about everything.

choices.text: Teach it to gather for itself, early

effects.log: You take it to the groves and show it a seed-head, and it looks at you as if you were very slow, and finds three more by itself. It is going to be fine.

choices.text: Let your mate teach it; watch them both

effects.log: Your mate teaches it everything, very patiently, and the chick ignores everything and learns it anyway. You have never seen your mate so happy, or so tired.

events.text: Years pass. The chick is no longer drab: one blue feather, then the rest. One morning it sings on the highest branch, not to you, and not to nobody, but out, toward the south. Toward a mountain of gold and jade, and a cave with red sand on its floor, that it has never seen and knows exactly how to find.

choices.text: Let it go without a word

effects.log: It goes at sunrise, south, a little crooked at first, then straight. It does not look back. Neither did you. You sit on the branch where it slept until noon.

choices.text: Fly with it to the edge of the land you know, and turn back there

effects.log: You fly beside it for three days, and on the fourth, at the coast, you stop on a rock and it does not. You watch it out of sight over the sea. (-5 health)

choices.text: Sing it the whole song once, both halves, before it goes

effects.log: It sits still for the whole song, the first time it has sat still in its life. Then it goes. Somewhere, centuries from now, on a ridge you will never see, it will sing that song, turned the other way round, and something will answer.

events.text: It is not one grove that flowers this time. It is all of them. From the south coast to the northern hills, every stem of one bamboo on the whole peninsula is in pale flower at once, as if a single order had gone out. The seed falls like rain. You have never seen so much. Neither has anyone, for a hundred years.

choices.text: Gather, and fill every hollow tree you know

effects.log: You gather all season. Every hollow tree, every crack in every cliff. The store will last you for generations. Behind you, mile after mile, the bamboo begins to die standing.

choices.text: Gather only what you need, and watch

effects.log: You take a little and watch the rest fall. Something is wrong with so much plenty. The rats are coming out of the ground in the evenings now, more than you have ever seen.

choices.text: Gather with your mate, and sing while you work

effects.log: A whole season in the falling seed, two voices in the yellowing groves. It is the best season of your life. You will not be able to think of it, later, without thinking of what came after.

events.text: The bamboo is dead from coast to hills. The seed is eaten. And the rats, who multiplied on it all year, have come down out of the dead groves in brown rivers, at night, into the paddies and the barns. They eat the standing rice. They eat the seed-rice in the jars. In the villages, people sit up all night with sticks.

choices.text: Hunt the rats beside the village cats, every night

effects.log: A phoenix does not hunt. You hunt. Nobody in the villages ever believes it afterward, the five-coloured bird in the barn with a rat in its beak. (-8 health, -2 purity)

choices.text: Call the owls and the hawks to the villages

effects.log: You go to every owl and hawk in three provinces, even the owls that guard their rotten rats, and ask. They come. The owls cannot believe their luck. For one season the owl is almost pleasant.

choices.text: Keep away. It is the way of bamboo, and of rats

effects.log: You keep to the high ridges. From up there the villages look the same as ever. They are not.

events.text: Famine. The first winter after the rats, the villages under your ridge eat the seed-rice, then the bark of the elms, then nothing. A child sits under your paulownia every evening, too weak to climb, and looks up. Your store of bamboo seed, in the hollow tree above the child's head, would feed that whole household until spring.

choices.text: Share it. Tip the hollow tree out onto the child's doorstep

effects.log: The family wakes to a doorstep heaped with seed, pale and strange. They do not know what it is. They cook it. It is enough. In the spring the child plants a paulownia, with its own hands, for no reason it can explain.

choices.text: Share half, and keep half

effects.log: Half the store, on half the doorsteps. It is not enough, quite. It is a great deal more than nothing. You lie awake in the hollow tree beside the half you kept.

choices.text: Keep it. You will need it in the lean years

effects.log: You keep it. The child stops coming in the second month. You eat the seed through the lean years after, and it tastes of nothing at all, and you were right that you would need it.

events.text: The lean years come, as you knew they would after so much giving. The store is thin, and the bamboo will not flower again for a generation. Your crop aches. Below in the farmyards the millet smells of everything you are not allowed to want.

choices.text: Fast, and fly on

effects.log: A phoenix may fly a thousand li hungry. You fly two thousand. It is very cold. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck a little millet, just this once

effects.log: It tastes like a farmyard. It is food. A sparrow beside you on the threshing floor looks at you sideways and says nothing, very loudly. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Your mate offers you their seed. Refuse, and share what is left equally

effects.log: You split the last of the seed down the middle, one grain at a time, on a flat stone, the two of you, very carefully. It is not enough for either. It is exactly half. (-5 health)

events.text: Twenty years after the famine. The grey dead bamboo has fallen and new green shoots are coming up through it, thin and everywhere. And in every village under your ridge, beside the threshing floors, there are young paulownias, planted the winter of the hunger by people who could not have told you why.

choices.text: Visit every one of them

effects.log: A year of visiting trees. In each village, an old person comes out and looks up at you and nods, as if an appointment has been kept. Nobody says the word famine.

choices.text: Sit only in the tree the child planted

effects.log: The child is grown, with children. They come out at dawn and look at you in the tree they planted, and you look back, and neither of you needs to say anything.

events.text: The store is empty. The last hollow tree, the last crack in the cliff: nothing but husks. Below, the palace granary is full of millet, and the court that once begged you to come would scatter a whole cartload of it on the terrace if you only landed there.

choices.text: Fast

effects.log: You fast on the branch. You have fasted before. You are older now, and it is longer. (-10 health)

choices.text: Peck millet from a farmyard far from the court, where nobody knows you

effects.log: A farmyard three valleys off. Nobody sees but the hens, who are offended. You fly home full and ashamed. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Let your mate give you their share

effects.log: Your mate pushes their last seed toward you with their beak and will not hear a word. You eat it. They grow thin over the winter. You watch them grow thin.

variants: Husks. Every store you keep, the hollow trees, the cracks in the cliff, holds nothing but husks this winter. Far below, the palace granary is full, and the court would heap millet on the terrace for you in an hour.

The thin year comes again, and finds your stores empty. Down in the capital the granary doors stand open, and everyone knows the court would scatter millet for you by the cartload, if you would only land.
Snow on the paulownia, and nothing in the hollow but frost. The court below has millet enough to feed a province, and has never stopped hoping you will come down and eat it.

events.text: The Lean Year, and this time the whole land knows it. The court has heard that the phoenix is hungry. On the palace terrace, in full sight of your roof, a silver dish has been set out, heaped with the finest millet in the kingdom, husked by hand. A herald stands beside it. He has clearly been told to wait as long as it takes.

choices.text: Fast, in full sight of the dish

effects.log: You sit on the roof all winter and do not look at the dish. The whole capital watches the phoenix not eat. It becomes a proverb by spring. The herald is given a pension. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly far away to fast where the dish cannot see you

effects.log: You fast in the hills. The herald waits until the millet goes mouldy, then is quietly reassigned. (-10 health)

choices.text: Eat from the dish

effects.log: You come down and eat. The court is overjoyed: heaven has accepted the reign's offering. You fly back up to the roof with millet in your crop and the whole capital whispering. (-8 purity)

events.text: No seed, and snow. The small birds that settle where you settle have come to your tree in their hundreds, and they have found you out: you are hungry too. A flock of buntings lands on the branch with millet in their beaks, one grain each, and lay them along the branch beside you in a neat line, and wait.

choices.text: Thank them, and eat none of it

effects.log: You bow to each bunting. They are not offended. They eat the millet themselves, which was always the plan, and stay on the branch all night to keep you warm. (-10 health)

choices.text: Eat one grain from each, so they are not shamed

effects.log: One grain from each beak. It is not much millet. It is a great deal of courtesy. Your breast feathers know the difference, and charge you for the millet anyway. (-4 purity)

choices.text: Let your mate eat it. They are thinner than you

effects.log: Your mate will not. You will not. In the end the buntings eat it, and the two of you sit in a row of small birds all night, and it is warm. (-10 health)

events.text: Word on the wind, from bird to bird, faster than any herald: the bamboo of the southern province is in flower. All of it, all at once. The small birds who follow you are already lifting from the hedges, waiting to see which way you turn.

choices.text: Turn south at once, and gather

effects.log: You are in the flowering groves by the next dawn, with half the birds of the north behind you. You gather for a season. The store will last a long time.

choices.text: Go south, but warn the villages near the groves about the rats that will come

effects.log: You gather, and in the evenings you fly low over the bamboo villages, again and again, until an old woman in one of them understands, and starts the whole province mending its grain jars.

choices.text: Let the others gather first. There is plenty

effects.log: The small birds go first, then the pheasants, then you. There is plenty. There is so much that it frightens you a little.

events.text: The southern bamboo is in flower, and the bamboo-cutters of the south have noticed what follows it. A whole village has climbed into the flowering grove with drums and nets, because a phoenix's feather sells for a year's rice to the crown-makers, and everybody knows where the phoenix goes when the bamboo flowers.

choices.text: Gather at night, in the dark, and be gone by dawn

ok.log: Three nights of gathering by moonlight with the drums silent below. You are gone before the cutters wake. They find husks, and a single five-coloured down feather, and fight over it.

fail.log: A drum goes off right under you. Nets. You get away with half a crop of seed and a torn wing. (-10 health)

choices.text: Find a grove nobody knows, far up a gorge

effects.log: Up a gorge where nobody goes, a single stand of bamboo in flower. Less seed. No drums.

choices.text: Land in front of the village in full sight and look at the nets until they are put down

effects.log: It takes most of the morning. One by one the nets are lowered. An old woman says something sharp to the headman, and the drums go home. You gather in peace, watched by a hundred silent people.

events.text: Drums in the capital. A new ruler holds the land below. The heralds are on every road saying heaven smiles on the reign; they always say that. In the palace, you know without looking, somebody is already asking the court musicians whether they can play the Shao.

choices.text: Look first at the granaries and the prisons, before the throne

effects.log: The granaries are as they were. The prisons are as they were. Nothing has changed yet. You will watch, and the springs will decide in their own time.

choices.text: Look at the face of the new ruler on the gate tower

effects.log: Young, or old, or frightened, or not: from a ridge you can see only that the face is turned up, at the sky, looking for you. Every one of them does that.

choices.text: Ask your mate what they make of the drums

effects.log: Your mate listens to the drums a long time. "Too loud," your mate says. "Or not loud enough. It is too soon to say." That is your mate all over, and it is also true.

events.text: A new reign, and the first decree of the new ruler is pinned to every gate in the capital: paulownias are to be planted in every county seat, so that the phoenix will find a place to rest. Ten thousand saplings are ordered from the nurseries. The farmers who have to dig the holes are not consulted.

choices.text: Be pleased. Trees are trees

effects.log: In a few years there are paulownias in every county seat, and you rest in a few of them, and say nothing either way. The ruler takes the silence for approval. It was only rest.

choices.text: Note who was not consulted

effects.log: A ruler who orders trees for a bird and holes for the farmers is telling you something early. You remember it. It does not mean what you think yet.

events.text: A new reign. The old ruler's body is carried out of the north gate, and the new one is carried in at the south, and between the two, on the empty road for a moment, there is nobody at all. The small birds of the whole capital have gone quiet. They are waiting to see where you settle.

choices.text: Settle nowhere yet. Let the birds wait with you

effects.log: You stay on the far ridge, and the birds of the capital stay restless, and the new court notices that its hedges are empty. It is a good thing for a court to notice early.

choices.text: Settle on the old ruler's tomb mound for one day, out of respect

effects.log: A day on the grass of the new tomb. The birds of the capital follow you out of the city to the mound, and the mourners walk home through a city without a single sparrow in it.

events.text: Your mate has watched this court with you a whole season, and has decided: the ruler is not worthy. They will not be talked round. You are not sure they are right. You are not sure they are wrong. They sit on the far end of the ridge-tile, which is a long way, for a pair.

choices.text: Watch another season before you decide anything

effects.log: Another season. You both watch. Neither of you speaks of it. It is the most companionable disagreement you have ever had.

choices.text: Tell them you trust your own eyes

effects.log: Your mate says nothing at all, and flies to the next roof, and sleeps there. In the morning they are back. They always come back. It does not make it easier.

choices.text: Tell them you trust theirs

effects.log: Your mate looks at you, startled, and then moves along the ridge-tile, closer, until your wings touch. "I might be wrong," they say. "I know," you say.

events.text: The ruler your mate thought unworthy, the one you came in the dance for anyway, has turned out exactly as your mate said. The prisons are full again. Your mate has not said a word about it in a year. That is worse than anything they could say.

choices.text: Say it first: "You were right"

effects.log: "I know," your mate says. And then, after a long time: "I wish I had not been." You sit together on the branch until it is dark.

choices.text: Say nothing. Leave the land together, now

effects.log: You do not say it. You go up off the roof together at noon in full sight, and that says it for you. (Leave the Land; the reign will read it.)

events.text: The widowed years. When you watch a court now, you hear in your head what your mate would have said about it, and you are not sure, any more, whether it is memory or only the wind. Today the voice says: not worthy. Your own eyes are not sure.

choices.text: Trust the voice

effects.log: You do not come in the dance. Years later the reign goes bad, as the voice said. Or it goes bad because reigns do. You will never know, and you find that you can live with that.

choices.text: Trust your own eyes. They are the only ones you have now

effects.log: You watch another season, alone, and decide alone. It is harder. It is also, you realise, what the Lone Vow was for.

events.text: You come down from the eaves at night in the shape that can speak and sit on the step of the palace granary. The keeper, {npc}, is counting sacks by lantern and talks to you as if you were another clerk who could not sleep. "Full," {npc} says. "Full as an egg. And the county granaries empty. Guess why."

choices.text: "Tell me why"

effects.log: "Because they count the palace granary when a phoenix is due," {npc} says, "and nobody counts the counties." {He} looks at you a moment too long. "Somebody should," {he} says.

choices.text: "Open the county granaries, then. You have the keys"

mem.note: told me to open the granaries

effects.log: {npc} laughs. Then {he} does not laugh. "Only one," {he} says. "Only one key." The next winter, one county granary is open, and nobody can find out who did it.

choices.text: Help {him} count, sack by sack

mem.note: helped me count the sacks all night

effects.log: You count until dawn. The count is wrong by forty sacks, in the ruler's favour. {npc} writes the true number, and looks at you, and you both know what it means.

events.text: The night jailer of the palace prison, {npc}, smokes a pipe on the wall at midnight and does not mind company. "Three hundred inside," {npc} says. "Two hundred and ninety did nothing at all. Ten did something, and of those ten, four are here because they did it to the wrong family." {He} spits over the wall. "You want to know what a ruler is? Ask a jailer."

choices.text: "Then I am asking"

mem.note: asked me on the wall what a ruler is

effects.log: {npc} tells you all night. Names, families, the price of a release. By dawn you know this court better than its own ministers. The jailer goes home to bed, very pleased with {his} night.

choices.text: "Let two of them out tonight. I will be the omen that explains it"

mem.note: took the blame for the open cell

effects.log: In the morning there is a phoenix on the prison roof and a cell door open and two farmers gone home. The court calls it a miracle. {npc} calls it a good night. You are less sure it was clean. (-2 purity)

events.text: A court musician, {npc}, practising alone in the music hall long after midnight, stops when you come in from the dark in the shape that can speak and sit down among the stone chimes. "They want the Shao for the new year," {npc} says, "to call the phoenix. I have told them I can play the notes. I cannot play the music. Nobody can, for a court that has to ask."

choices.text: "Play me the notes, then"

mem.note: heard me play the Shao alone

effects.log: {npc} plays the first movement alone in the dark hall. It is beautiful, and it is only notes. "You hear it?" {he} says. You do. You stay for all nine, and {npc} plays the ninth for you as {he} will never play it for the court.

choices.text: "Then play it badly, so they learn to stop asking"

mem.note: told me to play it badly

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard {he} has to sit down on the stone chimes, which make a noise like a temple falling over. At the new year {he} plays the Shao perfectly, out of pride, and you do not come, out of principle.

events.text: A child ruler, {npc}, nine years old, cannot sleep, and has crept out of the royal bedchamber onto the veranda in a quilt to look at the moon, and finds you sitting on the rail. {npc} is not frightened. Children rarely are, of you. "Are you the phoenix?" {npc} asks. "The regent says you will come if I am good. What is good?"

choices.text: "Feeding people. Letting the innocent go home. Telling the truth when it costs you"

effects.log: {npc} repeats it three times, very seriously, to remember it. Thirty years later a ruler opens the granaries in a flood without waiting for a minister's permission, and says, when asked why, that a bird told {him} to on a veranda.

choices.text: "Good is not what the regent says it is"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about that for a long time, in the quilt. "I thought so," {he} says at last. "I just wanted somebody to say it." You stay on the rail until the child falls asleep.

choices.text: Say nothing. Sing very softly until the child sleeps

effects.log: {npc} is asleep before the second verse. In the morning the child will not be sure it happened. That is all right. Some of the best things a ruler learns, they are not sure ever happened.

events.text: An old court lady, {npc}, has fed the sparrows of the inner palace every morning for fifty years with crumbs from {his} own breakfast. Tonight {he} finds you on the wall above the sparrows' corner, in the shape that can speak, and offers you a crumb too, out of habit, and then looks at you properly and laughs. "No," {npc} says. "You would not. Of course. Do you want to know what the sparrows told me about this court?"

choices.text: "Very much"

effects.log: The sparrows, it turns out, know everything: who eats alone, who is visited at night, which minister has a cough that is not a cough. {npc} has been listening to them for fifty years. Nobody ever asked {him}.

choices.text: Take the crumb, and give it to the sparrows yourself

effects.log: The sparrows come down onto the wall, very nervous, and take the crumb from your beak one at a time. {npc} watches with {his} hand over {his} mouth. It is the best morning of {his} fifty years in the palace, and {he} tells nobody.

events.text: A young censor, {npc}, newly appointed to the office that tells the ruler unwelcome truths, is sitting on the steps of the censorate with a memorial in {his} lap that will probably end {his} career. When you sit down beside {him} in the shape that can speak, {npc} hands it to you without a word. It is about the palace springs. It says they have begun to taste of iron.

choices.text: "Submit it. It is true"

mem.note: told me to submit the memorial

effects.log: {npc} submits it in the morning. {He} is exiled to the coast by the end of the month, and the memorial is read aloud in every wineshop in the capital by the end of the year. The springs go on tasting of iron. Now everyone knows it.

choices.text: "Wait a year. Make it impossible to ignore, then submit"

mem.note: told me to wait and gather proof

effects.log: A year of tasting springs and writing down dates. The memorial {npc} submits is so complete that the ruler cannot exile {him} without exiling every fact in it. It is not acted on. It is not forgotten.

choices.text: Taste the palace spring yourself, at dawn, to know

effects.log: You taste it at dawn. {npc} watches your face from the steps and reads it before you speak. "So," {he} says, and tears up nothing, and submits it.
